title: The Morning Build for July 3, 2026: AI Compute Sales, Edge Devices, and Data Privacy Policy
intro: Big AI players are shifting from model-only strategies to selling compute, prototyping edge devices, and pushing rules about how web data is used for training. These moves change where revenue, hardware, and legal control sit in the AI stack.
meta_description: Big AI firms plan to sell spare compute, SpaceX shows an AI handset prototype, U.S. order bans differential privacy, and Cloudflare blocks mixed-use crawlers.

stories.headline: Meta plans a Meta Compute cloud to sell excess AI compute and hosted models
stories.what_happened: Bloomberg reported Meta is developing a cloud infrastructure business, called Meta Compute, to sell AI compute capacity and hosted models including Muse Spark; the initiative is led by Santosh Janardhan, Daniel Gross, and Dina Powell McCormick. The report follows SpaceX/xAI moves to lease excess datacenter capacity and notes Meta has committed $182.9 billion to AI infrastructure spending as of Q1.
stories.why_it_matters: If Meta offers raw compute and hosted models on its own datacenters, it becomes a direct competitor to AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure and changes who monetizes AI investment: owners of physical capacity. This affects procurement and deployment choices for engineers who currently rely on hyperscaler compute pools.
stories.outlook: Watch whether Meta announces pricing, customer contracts, or a public product launch that clarifies how its offering will differ from existing cloud and GPU-leasing players.

stories.headline: SpaceX showed investors a handset-like AI device prototype tied to xAI tech
stories.what_happened: Reports say SpaceX displayed a sleeker-than-iPhone, handset-like prototype intended to run a proprietary OS and integrate xAI; Elon Musk denied the reporting. The device was shown privately to investors and SpaceX said the design could still change.
stories.why_it_matters: A handset-style device running native xAI code and a proprietary OS would signal SpaceX intends to control both hardware and on-device AI software, which matters to engineers planning client-side model deployment and OS-level integrations.
stories.outlook: Monitor SpaceX and xAI for product announcements, developer documentation, or confirmations that clarify hardware specs and the device’s intended production path.

stories.headline: DAO 216-26 directive bans differential privacy and noise infusion for Census and BEA publications
stories.what_happened: A guest post collected by Scott Aaronson reports that the U.S. Secretary of Commerce issued DAO 216-26 on June 4, 2026, restricting disclosure avoidance to coarsening and suppression and forbidding noise infusion methods and differential privacy for BEA and Census Bureau publications.
stories.why_it_matters: The directive removes modern noise-infusion techniques that have enabled granular but privacy-protected datasets, which will force agencies to coarsen data or publish less, affecting engineers and researchers who rely on fine-grained federal data.
stories.outlook: Expect debate and potential pushback from the scientific community and civil servants about data utility and confidentiality as agencies adapt to the new rules.

stories.headline: Cloudflare will block mixed-use crawlers by default and push publishers to charge AI bots
stories.what_happened: Cloudflare announced default settings, effective September 15, 2026, that block mixed-use crawlers on pages that host ads unless site owners change settings. The company said it will apply the change to new customers, new sites by existing customers, and existing free customers, and is evolving Pay Per Crawl into Pay Per Use with partners Ceramic.ai and You.com.
stories.why_it_matters: Default blocking of mixed-use crawlers will force AI model providers to separate search crawlers from training and agent crawlers or get explicit publisher opt-in, affecting how engineers obtain web content for training and agent services and introducing new potential cost paths for data access.
stories.outlook: Watch adoption of Cloudflare’s Pay Per Use flows and whether AI providers rearchitect crawlers or negotiate publisher-level agreements.

narration_script: Meta is preparing a cloud business called Meta Compute to sell excess AI compute and hosted models, according to reporting that cites internal planning led by infrastructure leaders Santosh Janardhan, Daniel Gross, and Dina Powell McCormick. The report notes Meta has committed $182.9 billion to AI infrastructure and that the plan follows SpaceX and xAI moves to lease idle datacenter capacity. For engineers, a Meta-owned compute offering would position a major platform as a direct supplier of raw GPUs and hosted models, changing procurement options currently dominated by hyperscalers. Watch for product details, pricing, and customer contracts to see how Meta’s offering will compare to AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure. SpaceX also showed investors a handset-like AI prototype tied to xAI and a proprietary operating system, though Elon Musk denied the reporting and the company says the design could change. If SpaceX products ship with native xAI software and a proprietary OS, that will affect how teams plan on-device model execution and OS-level integrations. The U.S. Commerce Department issued DAO 216-26, which restricts disclosure avoidance to coarsening and suppression and forbids noise infusion and differential privacy for Census and BEA publications. The directive removes modern noise-infusion methods that enabled fine-grained, privacy-protected federal datasets, and the guest post warns agencies will have to coarsen data or publish less. Engineers and researchers who rely on granular federal statistics should expect reduced data utility and a period of policy and technical pushback. Finally, Cloudflare will block mixed-use crawlers by default on ad-hosting pages starting September 15, 2026, and is shifting Pay Per Crawl toward Pay Per Use with partners Ceramic.ai and You.com. That default forces AI providers to separate search crawling from training and agent crawling or secure publisher opt-ins, which may add cost or engineering work to how web content is gathered for models. Together these stories show compute, hardware, and data rules moving to the center of AI business models and engineering plans. Follow product launches from Meta and SpaceX, legal and technical responses to DAO 216-26, and how AI firms adapt crawlers and publisher payment models to Cloudflare’s defaults.
